title: Stuffed cabbage with meat, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed cabbage with meat, Puerto Rican style is a classic dish of Puerto Rican cuisine that consists of cabbage leaves wrapped around a mixture of ground beef, pork, rice, tomatoes, onion, and characteristic spices such as adobo, oregano, and cumin. It is simmered in a fragrant tomato‑based broth until the cabbage is tender.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish blends Spanish colonial culinary heritage with local Caribbean flavors.
In Puerto Rico cabbage is often used instead of traditional banana leaves, making the recipe more accessible.
Stuffed cabbage is commonly served at holidays and family celebrations as a symbol of abundance.
The rice in the filling is usually toasted first to keep it fluffy after cooking.
Traditional sauce may contain a splash of vinegar, giving the dish a subtle tang.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and pork supply vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from cabbage and rice
items.content: Cabbage leaves and whole‑grain rice aid digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and spices (adobo, oregano) are rich in antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains iron, zinc, and potassium, important for immune function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The sauce often includes added salt and soy sauce, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Meat fat
items.content: Pork can be fatty; lean cuts or reduced amounts can be used for a lighter version.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some spices (e.g., cumin) may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Tomato acidity
items.content: Tomatoes increase acidity, which may be problematic for those with ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, garnished with fresh cilantro or parsley. A squeeze of lime adds brightness. It pairs well with rice, beans, or crusty bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove or in the microwave, adding a splash of broth to prevent drying out.
